name: Jewish communities
subtitle: of the Arab world & Iran
native_language: Judeo-Arabic, Ladino, Judeo-Farsi, Aramaic (Babylonian), Yemenite Hebrew
native_script: Hebrew/Aramaic square script; Judeo-Arabic in Hebrew letters
current_script: Hebrew in Israel; diaspora communities maintain heritage languages
arabization_status: N/A — communities expelled before full Arabization; Hebrew maintained as sacred language continuously
language_vitality: Endangered in diaspora; Judeo-Arabic and Ladino critically endangered

key_destruction_events.event: Farhud pogrom, Baghdad — 180 Jews killed in two days, the largest massacre of Jews in an Arab country
Arab-Israeli War triggers simultaneous pogroms, citizenship revocations, and property seizures across nine Arab countries
Nasser expels Egyptian Jews after Suez Crisis; property nationalized; 75,000 → fewer than 100 within a decade
Gaddafi seizes Libya — last Jews expelled; property confiscated; community of 38,000 → 0
Last Jew in Afghanistan (Zebulon Simantov) departs Kabul as Taliban enter

human_scale_fact: Jews had lived continuously in Babylon (Iraq) for 2,600 years — since the destruction of the First Temple in 586 BCE. They predate Islam in that land by over a millennium. Operation Magic Carpet (1949–50) airlifted 49,000 Yemenite Jews to Israel in 380 flights. Most had never seen an airplane.
key_quote: We did not leave. We were made to leave. There is a difference — and that difference matters to history.
key_quote_attribution: Shlomo Hillel, Iraqi-Jewish statesman and diplomat
israel_connection: Israel was founded in part as refuge for expelled Jewish communities; 850,000+ Jewish refugees from Arab lands resettled there — a displacement larger than the Palestinian refugee crisis, with no UN agency and no international compensation

resources.label: Jewish Virtual Library — Jewish communities in Arab countries
JIMENA — Jews Indigenous to the Middle East and North Africa
Divan — Sephardic and Mizrahi cultural preservation

name: Eastern Christian communities
subtitle: Coptic, Maronite, Greek Orthodox, Melkite
note_on_numbers: Absolute numbers grew (especially Copts) but share of MENA population collapsed from ~20% to ~4%
native_language: Coptic (Egypt), Syriac/Aramaic (Iraq/Syria), Armenian, Greek, Arabic
native_script: Coptic alphabet (modified Greek), Syriac Estrangela script, Armenian script, Greek
current_script: Arabic largely imposed for daily life; liturgical languages maintained in church
arabization_status: Significant — Coptic language reduced to liturgy only; Syriac endangered; Greek Orthodox Arabized in language but not identity
language_vitality: Coptic: dormant (liturgical only). Syriac: endangered. Armenian: vulnerable.

key_destruction_events.event: Armenian Genocide — Ottoman forces kill 600,000–1.5 million Armenians; concurrent Assyrian Seyfo — first genocide of 20th century
Istanbul pogrom — coordinated mob violence destroys Greek Orthodox community; Greeks: 100,000 → 3,000
US invasion of Iraq — church bombings begin; 1.5 million Iraqi Christians start their exodus
Our Lady of Salvation church bombing, Baghdad — 58 worshippers killed during Mass
ISIS issues 'convert, pay, or die' ultimatum to Nineveh Plains Christians — emptied within days
UN formally declares ISIS actions against Christians an act of genocide

human_scale_fact: Egypt's Coptic Church was founded by St. Mark in 42 CE — 600 years before Islam reached Egypt. Iraq's Christian population fell from 1.5 million in 2003 to under 200,000 today — an 87% collapse in 20 years driven not by one event but by sustained bombing, kidnapping, and murder.
key_quote: Our language is Aramaic — the language Jesus spoke. We have been here since before the caliphate, before the crusades, before Islam. We are not a remnant. We are the original people.
israel_connection: ~180,000 Arab Christians hold full Israeli citizenship. Nazareth — majority-Christian Arab city — is stable and growing. The only Arabic-speaking Christian community in the Middle East not in demographic freefall.

resources.label: Aid to the Church in Need — country reports

name: Assyrian & Syriac people
subtitle: an ethnic nation without a state
native_language: Neo-Aramaic (Assyrian, Chaldean, Turoyo dialects) — the closest living language to what Jesus spoke
native_script: Syriac script (Estrangela, Serto, East Syriac) — one of the oldest continuously used alphabets in the world
current_script: Arabic imposed in Iraq/Syria for all official purposes; Syriac maintained in church and diaspora
arabization_status: Severe — Assyrian place names Arabized; Syriac schools closed or restricted; Kurdish regions partially more tolerant
language_vitality: Endangered — estimated 500,000–800,000 speakers globally, majority in diaspora

key_destruction_events.event: Seyfo (Assyrian genocide) — Ottoman and Kurdish forces kill 250,000–750,000 Assyrians; 'Seyfo' means 'sword' in Syriac
Simele massacre — Iraqi army kills 600+ Assyrian civilians in northern Iraq under British-mandated government
US invasion — Assyrian Christians specifically targeted as 'Crusaders' by Al-Qaeda and later ISIS
ISIS conquers Nineveh Plains — the Assyrian heartland for 3,000 years — emptied in days; churches dynamited

human_scale_fact: The Assyrian language (Neo-Aramaic) is a direct descendant of the language spoken by Jesus of Nazareth. The Syriac script is older than the Arabic alphabet. The Nineveh Plains — site of the ancient Assyrian Empire capital — has been continuously inhabited for 7,000 years. It was emptied in 72 hours in August 2014.
key_quote: We are not refugees. We are indigenous. Nineveh is ours — not from yesterday, but from 7,000 years ago.
israel_connection: Small Assyrian community in Israel; Aramaic-speaking villages in Galilee (Jish/Gush Halav) maintain liturgical Aramaic

resources.label: Hannibal Travis: Genocide in the Middle East (2010)

name: Armenian people
subtitle: survivors of the first genocide of the 20th century
note_on_numbers: Survivors in Turkey; global Armenian diaspora ~8 million worldwide; homeland Republic of Armenia established 1991
native_language: Armenian (Eastern and Western dialects)
native_script: Armenian alphabet — invented by Mesrop Mashtots in 405 CE; one of the most distinctive scripts in the world
current_script: Armenian script maintained by diaspora communities; Turkish Armenians historically forced to use Latin/Ottoman script
arabization_status: Minimal — Armenians maintained script and language through diaspora institutions; Turkey attempted Turkification not Arabization
language_vitality: Western Armenian (diaspora): endangered. Eastern Armenian (Republic of Armenia): healthy.

key_destruction_events.event: Armenian Genocide — Ottoman government systematically kills 600,000–1.5 million Armenians via death marches, mass shootings, and starvation; April 24 is Genocide Remembrance Day
Republic of Armenia briefly independent; Soviet annexation 1920
Lausanne Treaty — population exchanges expel remaining Armenians from Anatolia to Greece
Istanbul pogrom — Armenians among those targeted; community property destroyed
Republic of Armenia independent after Soviet collapse — first Armenian state since 1920

human_scale_fact: The Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem has been continuously inhabited since the 4th century CE — predating Islam, the Ottoman Empire, and modern Turkey. The Armenians were the first nation to adopt Christianity as a state religion (301 CE). Turkey officially denies the genocide that every major historian, the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and 32 countries recognize.
key_quote: They can kill us. They can exile us. They cannot kill our language. As long as one Armenian child reads our letters, we survive.
key_quote_attribution: Komitas Vardapet, Armenian composer and genocide survivor, 1915
israel_connection: Armenian Quarter in Jerusalem's Old City dates to 4th century CE; ~1,500 Armenians in Haifa; genocide survivors arrived in 1920s; Israel recognized Armenian Genocide in 2021

resources.label: Zoryan Institute for Contemporary Armenian Research
Houshamadyan — reconstruction of Ottoman Armenian life
Voices of the Armenians — USC Shoah Foundation

name: Yazidi people
subtitle: survivors of the 74th Ferman
native_language: Kurmanji Kurdish (primary); some speak Arabic
native_script: Modified Latin (in Turkey/diaspora); Arabic script (in Iraq); Kurdish Badini dialect
current_script: No distinct Yazidi script; use Kurdish scripts of host country
arabization_status: Significant in Iraq — Sinjar district Arabized under Saddam; place names changed; land redistributed to Arab tribes; Yazidis stripped of land rights
language_vitality: Kurmanji Kurdish: vulnerable; oral Yazidi religious texts (Kitêba Cilwe, Mishefa Reş) transmitted orally for centuries — now being transcribed

key_destruction_events.event: Seyfo — Ottoman forces massacre Yazidis alongside Assyrian Christians
Baathist Arabization — Yazidi villages forcibly displaced from Sinjar; land given to Arab settlers
Qahtaniya bombings — four coordinated truck bombs kill 796 Yazidis in deadliest terrorist attack in Iraq's history
August 3: ISIS captures Sinjar — 5,000+ men executed in one day; 7,000 women and girls sold in slave markets; 500,000 displaced onto Sinjar mountain
UN Commission of Inquiry formally declares ISIS actions against Yazidis constitute genocide

human_scale_fact: August 3, 2014 is commemorated as Yazidi Genocide Day. In Yazidi oral history, this was the 74th Ferman — the 74th attempt to eliminate them. Yazidi theology holds that they cannot convert others and cannot marry outside the faith: each person killed or enslaved is irreplaceable. The largest Yazidi community outside Iraq is now in Hanover, Germany — an ancient Mesopotamian mountain faith now practicing in European cities.
key_quote: They came because we are different. They called us devil worshippers. We who worship the Peacock Angel, who pray toward the sun. They came because we refused to be like them.
israel_connection: Israel accepted Yazidi refugees; formally recognized the Yazidi genocide while Arab League states were silent

resources.label: Nadia Murad — Nobel Peace Prize laureate and survivor testimony
UN Human Rights Council — They Came to Destroy (2016 report)

name: Zoroastrian people
subtitle: founders of Persian civilization
note_on_numbers: ~60,000 Parsis in India (descendants of medieval refugees); ~30,000 in diaspora USA/UK/Canada
native_language: Avestan (liturgical, extinct as spoken), Dari/Middle Persian (historical), modern Persian
native_script: Avestan script (liturgical); historically Pahlavi script; today use Persian script in Iran or Latin in diaspora
current_script: Arabic-based Persian script imposed in Iran; Avestan maintained only in liturgy
arabization_status: Complete Persianate → Arabized transition post-651 CE; Nowruz and many cultural traditions survived but Arabized vocabulary dominates modern Persian; Zoroastrian names increasingly rare
language_vitality: Avestan: extinct as spoken language (liturgical only). Dari: absorbed into modern Persian. Zoroastrian community languages: endangered.

key_destruction_events.event: Arab conquest of Persia — Zoroastrian state collapses; fire temples destroyed or converted to mosques; dhimmi status imposed
Mass conversion period — sustained social and economic pressure converts majority of Persians over 250 years
Zoroastrian refugees arrive in Gujarat, India — welcomed by local Hindu ruler; become the Parsi community
Islamic Revolution — Zoroastrian rights curtailed; fire temples restricted; converting to Zoroastrianism declared apostasy punishable by death

human_scale_fact: The Cyrus Cylinder (539 BCE) — the first declaration of human rights in recorded history — was authored by a Zoroastrian king. Nowruz (Persian New Year), celebrated by 300 million people worldwide, is a Zoroastrian holiday predating Islam by over a millennium. The religion that gave the world the concepts of heaven and hell, angels, and the cosmic struggle between good and evil now has fewer followers in its homeland than the population of a small American town.
key_quote: Good thoughts, good words, good deeds. Three words 3,500 years old. They may not survive another century in the land that created them.
key_quote_attribution: Zoroastrian creed — Humata, Hukhta, Huvarshta, c.1500 BCE
israel_connection: Zoroastrian pilgrims and scholars welcome; no indigenous community but open access unlike in Iran

resources.label: Federation of Zoroastrian Associations of North America

name: Mandaean (Gnostic) people
subtitle: the last living Gnostics
native_language: Mandaic (a dialect of Eastern Aramaic)
native_script: Mandaic script — a cursive alphabet derived from ancient Aramaic; one of the oldest continuously used scripts in the world
current_script: Mandaic maintained in liturgy and diaspora; Arabic imposed for all civil purposes in Iraq/Iran
arabization_status: Complete in civil life; Mandaic language and script survive only in religious texts and diaspora communities
language_vitality: Critically endangered — estimated fewer than 10,000 speakers worldwide; no country where it has official status

key_destruction_events.event: Arab conquest — Mandaeans' status under Islamic law uncertain; not clearly 'people of the book'; face periodic severe persecution
US invasion of Iraq — Mandaeans labelled 'pagans' by militias; targeted for kidnapping, forced conversion, and murder
UN formally reports Mandaeans face 'existential threat' in Iraq; mass flight begins
Last Mandaean silversmiths leave Baghdad — end of a guild tradition stretching back centuries

human_scale_fact: Mandaean theology requires baptism in flowing water (masbuta) which must be performed in a natural river or stream. As the community scatters to Western cities, their most sacred ritual becomes logistically impossible. Mandaeans are theologically pacifist — forbidden from bearing arms. In post-2003 Iraq, this made them uniquely defenseless. The largest Mandaean community in the world is now in Sydney, Australia — a religion of ancient Mesopotamian rivers, now practicing beside the Parramatta.
key_quote: We cannot convert others. We cannot marry outside our faith. We cannot replace those we lose. Each person who dies or is taken is a door that closes forever.
israel_connection: Small Mandaean community in Israel; able to practice river baptism in Jordan River and other waterways

name: Bahá'í people
subtitle: persecuted in their birthplace, headquartered in Israel
note_on_numbers: Stable in numbers but under severe apartheid-like conditions; global community 5–8 million
native_language: Persian (Farsi) — faith founded in Persia
native_script: Persian script; Bahá'í writings in Persian and Arabic
current_script: Persian/Arabic maintained; no distinct Bahá'í script
arabization_status: N/A — faith founded in Persian, not Arabic, cultural context; faces Islamization not Arabization
language_vitality: Persian: healthy as national language of Iran; Bahá'í specifically not a language community

key_destruction_events.event: Bahá'í Faith founded in Persia by the Báb — immediately persecuted by Qajar state and Shia clergy
The Báb publicly executed by firing squad in Tabriz; thousands of early followers killed in pogroms
Islamic Revolution — Bahá'í institutions banned; properties seized; National Spiritual Assembly members arrested and executed
Nine members of the elected Bahá'í National Spiritual Assembly executed without trial
Second National Spiritual Assembly elected; all nine members also executed
Bahá'í students banned from all Iranian universities — a ban maintained continuously to present day

human_scale_fact: Iran's constitution explicitly protects Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians as religious minorities. It does not mention Bahá'ís — leaving 300,000 people entirely outside legal protection. In response to the university ban, the community created the BIHE (Bahá'í Institute for Higher Education) — an underground university operating since 1987, with professors periodically arrested mid-semester. The House of the Báb in Shiraz — one of the holiest sites in the faith — was demolished by the Iranian government in 1979.
key_quote: They can take our buildings, our cemeteries, our jobs, our universities. They cannot take what we know to be true. We have been tested this way for 180 years.
israel_connection: Bahá'í World Centre — global spiritual and administrative headquarters — sits on Mount Carmel in Haifa; UNESCO World Heritage Site; explicitly chosen by Bahá'u'lláh; Iran executes Bahá'ís while their faith governs itself from the country Iran calls its enemy

resources.label: Iran Press Watch — Bahá'í persecution documentation
BIHE — Bahá'í Institute for Higher Education

name: Hindus & Sikhs of Afghanistan
subtitle: 3,500 years. Ended in a generation.
native_language: Dari (Afghan Persian), Pashto, Punjabi (Sikhs), Hindi
native_script: Gurmukhi (Sikhs), Devanagari (Hindus), Dari/Persian script for daily life
current_script: Arabic-based scripts imposed; Gurmukhi and Devanagari survive only in diaspora
arabization_status: Complete Islamization — Gandharan place names replaced; Sanskrit inscriptions destroyed; gurdwaras and temples demolished or converted; personal Hindu/Sikh names forbidden under Taliban
language_vitality: Dari and Pashto: healthy as Afghan national languages but stripped of Hindu/Sikh cultural content; Punjabi in diaspora: vulnerable

key_destruction_events.event: Mujahideen capture Kabul — systematic targeting of Hindu/Sikh minorities begins; property looted; temples desecrated
Taliban decree: all Hindus must wear yellow identification badges in public — explicitly echoing Nazi Germany
Brief reprieve under US-backed government; community emigrates steadily under continued harassment
Suicide bombing of Jalalabad Sikh delegation kills 19 Sikhs en route to meet President Ghani
Attack on Gurdwara Har Rai Sahib, Kabul — 25 Sikhs killed during morning prayers
Taliban return — last functioning gurdwara in Kabul closes; mass exodus of final families

human_scale_fact: From 220,000 people in 1992 to 27 in 2023 is a 99.99% decline in 31 years. There is no modern parallel for this speed and completeness of a community's erasure from a country. The Taliban yellow-badge decree for Hindus was explicitly compared by human rights organizations to the Nazi requirement that Jews wear yellow Stars of David. The last gurdwara in Afghanistan — Gurdwara Karte Parwan in Kabul, built in 1930 — closed permanently in 2021.
key_quote: My grandfather's grandfather was born in Kabul. His grandfather before him. We go back so far we have no memory of arriving — only of being here. Now there is no one left to remember that we were ever here at all.
israel_connection: No direct community; Afghan Hindu/Sikh diaspora primarily in India, UK, Canada

resources.label: Human Rights Watch — Afghanistan religious minorities

name: Kurdish people
subtitle: 40 million people — the largest ethnic group in the world without a state
note_on_numbers: Population not declining but rights, language, and land under continuous attack across all four host states
native_language: Kurmanji (Northern Kurdish), Sorani (Central Kurdish), Zazaki, Gorani
native_script: Modified Latin (Turkey, diaspora); Arabic-based (Iraq, Iran, Syria); Kurdish Latin alphabet standardized in 1932
current_script: Turkey: forced Latin script; all Kurdish-language education was banned until 2002; Iraq: Arabic script for Sorani; Iran: Arabic script; Syria: Arabic script
arabization_status: Severe in Syria (citizenship stripped 1962; Arabic names imposed; Kurdish schools banned) and Iraq (Saddam's Arabization of Kirkuk: Kurds expelled, Arabs settled). Turkification in Turkey. Persianization in Iran.
language_vitality: Kurmanji: vulnerable (15+ million speakers). Sorani: vulnerable (7+ million speakers). Zazaki: endangered. Gorani: critically endangered.

key_destruction_events.event: Sykes-Picot Agreement divides Kurdistan between four states — Kurds promised autonomy in Treaty of Sèvres (1920) but Lausanne Treaty (1923) eliminates this
Dersim massacre — Turkish army kills 13,000–70,000 Alevi Kurds; tens of thousands more deported
Syria strips 120,000 Kurds of citizenship overnight — made stateless by administrative decree
Saddam's Anfal campaign begins — chemical weapons used; 50,000–182,000 Kurds killed; 4,000 villages destroyed
Halabja chemical attack — Saddam uses nerve agents and mustard gas; 5,000 Kurds killed in one day
ISIS attacks Kurdish Kobane; Kurdish YPG/YPJ forces defend the city — Kurds become primary ground force against ISIS

human_scale_fact: The Halabja chemical attack on March 16, 1988 killed 5,000 Kurdish civilians in a single day — the largest chemical weapons attack against a civilian population in history. Saddam Hussein used nerve agents and mustard gas supplied in part by Western companies. The perpetrators were not prosecuted until 2007. Kurdish women fighters (YPJ) were among the primary forces that defeated ISIS on the ground — widely photographed worldwide, rarely given political recognition.
key_quote: They took our language first. Then our names. Then our villages. The map doesn't show Kurdistan. But we are still here.
israel_connection: Israel has historically maintained diplomatic and intelligence relations with Iraqi Kurds since 1960s; Israel supported Kurdish autonomy; small Kurdish Jewish community (Mizrahi) in Israel

name: Baloch people
subtitle: sitting on Pakistan's oil wealth, receiving none of it
note_on_numbers: Population not declining but subjected to enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and cultural suppression
native_language: Balochi (Western, Eastern, Southern dialects)
native_script: Arabic-based Balochi script (Nastaliq style); also written in Latin in diaspora
current_script: Urdu (Pakistan) and Farsi (Iran) imposed for all official purposes; Balochi excluded from education
arabization_status: Severe Urduization in Pakistan — Balochi banned from courts, government, and education; Balochistan's resources extracted by Punjabi-dominated federal government without consent or compensation
language_vitality: Endangered — no official status in any country; excluded from education systems in Pakistan and Iran

key_destruction_events.event: Kalat Khanate forcibly annexed by Pakistan — Khan of Kalat had declared independence; Baloch resistance begins
Zulfikar Ali Bhutto launches military operation against Baloch insurgency — 55,000 Pakistani troops deployed; thousands killed
Systematic enforced disappearances begin — over 6,000 documented missing persons; bodies later found with signs of torture
Nawab Akbar Bugti — paramount Baloch leader — killed by Pakistani military airstrike in his cave hideout
Human Rights Watch documents ongoing 'kill and dump' operations; Baloch bodies found with torture marks across Balochistan

human_scale_fact: Balochistan is Pakistan's largest province — 44% of total land area — but contains only 5% of the population, largely due to underdevelopment. The province produces 36% of Pakistan's natural gas and holds vast copper and gold reserves. Baloch communities receive almost no royalties or development. The Pakistani military has run enforced disappearance operations so systematic that 'missing persons' has become a defining feature of Baloch political life. Mothers of the disappeared march in Quetta carrying photographs of their sons — a scene documented by Human Rights Watch for two decades.
key_quote: They take our sons in the night. They return them in plastic bags, weeks later, with their fingernails pulled out. And the world calls this a counterterrorism operation.
key_quote_attribution: Voice of Baloch Missing Persons, Quetta, 2019
israel_connection: No direct connection; some Baloch diaspora advocate for Israeli recognition of their situation

name: Amazigh (Berber) people
subtitle: the indigenous people of North Africa — before the Arabs arrived
note_on_numbers: Population intact but identity, language, and culture systematically suppressed across the Maghreb for decades
native_language: Tamazight (umbrella term); major dialects: Tachelhit, Tarifit (Rif), Kabyle, Tamasheq (Tuareg), Tachawit
native_script: Tifinagh — one of the oldest scripts in the world; used by Tuareg continuously; recently revived across Maghreb
current_script: Arabic imposed for all official purposes across the Maghreb; Tifinagh officially adopted in Morocco (2011) and Algeria (2016) but implementation weak; Latin used in diaspora
arabization_status: Systematic Arabization since independence across all Maghrebi states — Amazigh excluded from schools, courts, media, and government until very recently; personal names Arabized; place names replaced with Arabic versions; Gaddafi banned all Berber cultural expression in Libya
language_vitality: Kabyle: vulnerable. Tachelhit: vulnerable. Tarifit: endangered. Tamasheq: endangered. Tachawit: critically endangered.

key_destruction_events.event: Algerian independence — Arabic declared sole national language despite majority Berber-speaking population; Amazigh identity criminalized
Berber Spring (Tafsut Imazighen) — student protests at University of Tizi Ouzou suppressed by Algerian army
Black Spring (Printemps Noir) — Kabyle protests after gendarmerie kills teenager; 126 protesters killed; 5,000 injured
Gaddafi falls — Libyan Amazigh emerge from 42 years of forced Arabization; speak openly for first time in decades
Algeria officially recognizes Tamazight as co-official national language — first Maghrebi state to do so

human_scale_fact: The Amazigh people were in North Africa for at least 10,000 years before the Arab conquest of 647 CE. Cleopatra was ethnically Macedonian Greek, not Egyptian — but the actual indigenous Egyptians of the ancient world were Berber-related populations. Gaddafi banned Amazigh names so completely that Libyan Berbers gave their children Arabic names publicly and Berber names secretly at home for 42 years. When Gaddafi fell in 2011, elderly Amazigh wept on camera — the first time in their lives they could speak their language in the street.
key_quote: They told us we were Arabs. They changed our names, our street signs, our history books. But you cannot change what a grandmother whispers to her grandchild in the dark.
israel_connection: Small Amazigh-Jewish community (descendants of Berber Jews who converted centuries ago) exists in Israel; Amazigh-Israeli cultural exchange has grown; some Amazigh activists explicitly support normalization with Israel

name: Nubian people
subtitle: flooded out of their homeland without consent
note_on_numbers: Population grew but displaced from ancestral homeland; 100,000 directly displaced by Aswan Dam; now 3 million in diaspora across Egypt and Sudan
native_language: Nobiin, Kenzi-Dongolawi, Midob (Nile Nubian languages)
native_script: Historically Meroitic script (extinct); Old Nubian (Coptic-based, liturgical); today uses Arabic script
current_script: Arabic fully imposed; Nobiin and other Nubian languages written in Arabic script if written at all; no official recognition in Egypt
arabization_status: Complete — Nubian languages excluded from all Egyptian education and public life; Nubian place names replaced with Arabic; the Nubian homeland itself no longer exists (submerged)
language_vitality: Nobiin: endangered (500,000 speakers). Kenzi-Dongolawi: endangered. Meroitic: extinct.

key_destruction_events.event: First Aswan Dam raises water levels — initial flooding of Nubian villages begins under British colonialism
Aswan High Dam completed — 100,000 Nubians forcibly relocated from their ancestral homeland (now submerged under Lake Nasser) without consent or adequate compensation
UNESCO rescues Abu Simbel temple complex but does not rescue living Nubian communities or their villages
Egypt's Article 236 of constitution promises Nubian return to homeland — never implemented; Nubian activists arrested for demanding enforcement

human_scale_fact: Nubia was a civilization older than Egypt — with its own pyramids, its own pharaohs (the 25th Dynasty, Nubian kings ruled all of Egypt 744–656 BCE), and its own script (Meroitic, still partially undeciphered). In 1964, Nasser flooded all of it — 500 km of the Nile Valley, 44 villages, archaeological sites stretching back 10,000 years — to build the Aswan High Dam. The Nubian people were moved to the desert. Egypt's constitution promises their return to the Nile. Egypt's government arrests them when they ask for it.
key_quote: My grandmother used to describe her house. The color of the door. The tree in the courtyard. The sound of the Nile at night. All of it is under water now. She never stopped describing it.
israel_connection: No direct community in Israel; Nubian issues largely outside Israeli political context

name: Alawite civilians
subtitle: a minority at existential risk — distinct from the Assad regime
note_on_framing: IMPORTANT: Alawite civilians are a religious minority at serious risk. The Assad family is Alawite. The Assad regime committed severe atrocities. These are separate facts. Both are true. The crimes of a regime do not justify collective punishment of a community.
native_language: Arabic (Syrian dialect)
native_script: Arabic script — fully Arabized
current_script: Arabic — Alawites do not have a distinct script tradition
arabization_status: Alawites are Arab-speaking; their distinctiveness is religious not linguistic; Alawite religious texts (partly secret) maintained in Arabic
language_vitality: N/A — Arabic is native language

key_destruction_events.event: Hama massacre by Assad's father — directed at Sunni Muslim Brotherhood but also reflects sectarian dynamics Alawites were embedded in
Syrian civil war — Alawites largely identified with Assad regime; complex civilian/combatant dynamics
Assad regime falls — Alawite civilians face reprisal killings by Sunni rebel groups; HTS and allied factions document massacre of Alawite villagers on Syrian coast
Mass killings of Alawite civilians reported in Latakia and Tartus countryside — UN calls for accountability

human_scale_fact: Alawites practice a syncretic faith incorporating elements of Shia Islam, Christianity (they celebrate Christmas and Easter), and ancient pre-Islamic Syrian religion. They were historically the poorest and most marginalized community in French Mandate Syria — the French deliberately recruited them into the military as a counterweight to Sunni Arab nationalism. The Assad family's rise to power used Alawite military positioning as its base — and now ordinary Alawite farmers and fishermen on the Syrian coast face being killed in their name.
key_quote: I never voted for Assad. My family never wanted this war. We are farmers. We are fishermen. But now they come to our villages and they kill us for his crimes.
israel_connection: Small Alawite community on Golan Heights; their situation complex given Israeli-Syrian border dynamics

resources.label: UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria

name: Circassian people
subtitle: survivors of Russia's forgotten genocide of 1864
note_on_numbers: Global Circassian diaspora 3–7 million (estimates vary widely); 700,000 is the figure for MENA countries specifically
native_language: Adyghe (West Circassian), Kabardian (East Circassian) — Northwest Caucasian language family
native_script: Cyrillic script (imposed in Soviet era); Latin-based scripts used in diaspora; no classical Circassian script survived
current_script: Arabic in Jordan/Syria; Hebrew in Israel; Cyrillic in Russia/Turkey; diaspora communities developing Latin-script revival
arabization_status: Significant — Circassians in Arab countries adopted Arabic for public life; Circassian language maintained in home and community but not transmitted to all younger generations
language_vitality: Adyghe: endangered (500,000 speakers). Kabardian: vulnerable (600,000 speakers). Both critically endangered outside Russia.

key_destruction_events.event: Russian conquest of Caucasus complete — Russo-Circassian War ends; Russian forces conduct mass expulsion; 75–90% of Circassian population (600,000–1.5 million) killed or expelled to Ottoman Empire
May 21 — Circassian Day of Mourning: mass deportation of survivors to Ottoman lands; thousands die at sea; this date commemorated as Circassian Genocide
Soviet collectivization — remaining Circassians in Caucasus face forced sedentarization and suppression of identity
Russia holds Sochi Winter Olympics on site of 1864 Circassian massacre and main deportation port — Circassian protests worldwide

human_scale_fact: The 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics were held on the exact site where, 150 years earlier, the final Circassian deportations took place — the beach from which hundreds of thousands of Circassians were loaded onto boats, many of which sank. Russia has never recognized the Circassian genocide. The Circassians in Jordan and Israel have maintained their language and identity better than those in Turkey, where 200 years of assimilation pressure has reduced many to 'Turks who dance Circassian dances at weddings.'
key_quote: On the Day of Mourning we do not celebrate. We remember 1864. We remember the boats. We remember the beach at Sochi that the Olympics tried to make us forget.
israel_connection: ~4,000–5,000 Circassians are full Israeli citizens in Kfar Kama and Rehaniya; male Circassians serve in IDF by community request since 1958; one of the best-preserved Circassian communities outside Russia

name: Ahwazi Arab people
subtitle: Arabic speakers in Iran — sitting on 80% of Iran's oil
native_language: Arabic (Khuzestani dialect)
native_script: Arabic script — same as official Iranian Arabic; but Arabic education banned in Iranian schools
current_script: Persian (Farsi) script imposed for all education and official purposes despite being Arabic speakers; Arabic education denied
arabization_status: Inverse — Ahwazis are Arab speakers facing Persianization; Arabic language banned from schools in Khuzestan; Persian names imposed on Arab towns and streets
language_vitality: Khuzestani Arabic: endangered in Iran due to institutional suppression; children educated only in Persian

key_destruction_events.event: Reza Shah Pahlavi annexes Arab sheikhdoms of Khuzestan — Arabic place names replaced with Persian; Arab identity suppressed
Islamic Revolution — Ahwazis briefly revolt expecting autonomy; Revolutionary Guards crush uprising; leaders executed
Letter leaked from Iranian vice-president proposing to 'dilute' Arab population by resettling non-Arabs in Khuzestan — massive protests; security crackdown kills 50+
Arab Spring inspires Ahwazi protests — suppressed by Revolutionary Guards; mass arrests of activists
Water protests — Khuzestan Ahwazis protest water diversion to Persian-majority provinces; at least 8 protesters killed

human_scale_fact: Khuzestan Province — the Ahwazi homeland — produces approximately 80% of Iran's oil and 60% of its gas. The Ahwazi Arab population lives in poverty while their land's resources fund the Iranian state. They cannot attend school in their own language. The rivers of their province are diverted to Persian-majority regions. In 2021, people were photographed drinking from muddy puddles in one of the world's most oil-rich regions.
key_quote: They tell us we are Iranian. But they teach our children in Persian. They take our water. They take our oil. They give us nothing. And then they arrest us for saying so.
key_quote_attribution: Ahwazi Arab activist, in exile, London, 2021
israel_connection: Ahwazi Arab activists have sometimes sought Israeli media coverage and political attention given Iran as common adversary; complex political dynamic

name: Dom people (Middle Eastern Roma)
subtitle: stateless, undocumented, invisible
note_on_numbers: Estimated — no census anywhere counts Dom population; extreme undercounting likely
native_language: Domari (Indo-Aryan language, related to Romani) — also called 'the language of Dom'
native_script: No classical script; Domari increasingly written in Arabic script; critically endangered
current_script: Arabic script used where written; most Dom are not formally literate
arabization_status: Complete in public life; Domari language suppressed by association with poverty and marginalization; many Dom hide their identity and speak only Arabic publicly
language_vitality: Critically endangered — estimated 500,000 speakers remaining; UNESCO lists as 'definitely endangered'

key_destruction_events.event: Dom migrate from Indian subcontinent to Middle East — origin in Northwest India related to but distinct from European Roma
Israeli-Arab wars displace Dom communities in Palestine/Jordan — already stateless, made further stateless
Arab Spring — Dom communities in Syria, Libya, Egypt particularly vulnerable as states collapse
ISIS targets Dom communities in Iraq and Syria as 'immoral' — musicians and entertainers specifically persecuted

human_scale_fact: The Dom are the 'other Roma' — the branch of the original Indian diaspora that migrated west through Persia and settled in the Middle East, while the European Roma continued into the Balkans. They share a common origin 1,000 years ago. In Lebanon, Dom children are frequently denied birth registration — making them stateless in the most literal sense: they do not legally exist. They cannot attend school, access healthcare, or cross borders. In Jordan, Dom are sometimes called 'Nawar' — a slur — and refused service in shops.
key_quote: We have no country. We have no papers. We have no rights. We have only our music. And in some places, they have taken that too.
israel_connection: Small Dom community in Israel; some receive citizenship; relatively better situation than in Arab states

name: Shia Muslims
subtitle: persecuted as heretics by co-religionists
note_on_numbers: ~15% of all Muslims globally; majority in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain; large minorities in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Kuwait
native_language: Arabic, Persian, Urdu — no distinct Shia language
native_script: Arabic script — same as Sunni communities
current_script: No distinction
arabization_status: N/A — Shia are Arabic speakers in Arab world; distinct suppression is religious, not linguistic
language_vitality: N/A

key_destruction_events.event: Battle of Karbala — Hussein ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet, killed by Umayyad forces; founding trauma of Shia Islam
Iranian Revolution creates Shia theocracy; Saudi Arabia responds by massively funding Wahhabi Sunni extremism globally — beginning of modern sectarian war
Mecca massacre — Saudi security forces kill 402 Iranian Shia pilgrims during Hajj
Post-Iraq invasion sectarian war — Al-Qaeda targets Shia mosques and markets; thousands killed

human_scale_fact: In Bahrain, Shia Muslims are 65–70% of the citizen population — a clear majority — yet are systematically excluded from the military, security services, and senior government positions by a Sunni monarchy backed by Saudi Arabia and the United States. In 2011, Bahraini Shia rose in peaceful protest during the Arab Spring; Saudi Arabia sent troops to suppress them. In Pakistan, Shia doctors, lawyers, and academics are targeted on 'kill lists' by Lashkar-e-Jhangvi — their names and professions circulated in leaflets, their murders carried out in broad daylight.
key_quote: We say the same shahada. We face the same Mecca. We fast the same Ramadan. And they say we are not Muslim. And then they kill us.
israel_connection: Iran is Shia theocracy and primary state sponsor of anti-Israel activity; Iraqi and Lebanese Shia militias armed by Iran fight against Israel; complex relationship — Shia civilians often caught between Iranian regime ambitions and their own interests

name: Ahmadi Muslims
subtitle: the only people in the world declared non-Muslim by constitutional amendment
native_language: Urdu, Punjabi, English
native_script: Urdu/Nastaliq script, Latin script
current_script: No restriction on script; restriction is on content — Ahmadis cannot write the kalima, cannot call their worship sites mosques, cannot use Islamic greetings
arabization_status: N/A — Ahmadis are South Asian, not Arab; persecution is religious identity suppression not Arabization
language_vitality: N/A

key_destruction_events.event: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad founds Ahmadiyya movement in Qadian, India, claiming to be the promised Messiah of Islam
Anti-Ahmadi riots in Pakistan — first major sectarian violence; hundreds killed; army martial law
Pakistani parliament amends constitution — officially declares Ahmadis non-Muslim; first time any country has defined who is and isn't Muslim by statute

Ordinance XX — Ahmadis forbidden from calling themselves Muslim, saying Assalamu Alaikum, displaying Quranic verses, or calling their places of worship mosques; criminal penalties up to 3 years imprisonment
Taliban attack two Ahmadi mosques simultaneously in Lahore — 86 killed at Friday prayers; deadliest attack on Ahmadis in history

human_scale_fact: Pakistan is the only country in the world that has legally defined a religious group as non-Muslim by constitutional amendment — a unique act of state-enforced excommunication. Ahmadi graves in Pakistan are regularly vandalized; epitaphs quoting the Quran must be removed or the family faces prosecution. In Indonesia, the world's largest Muslim-majority country, Ahmadis have been banned from preaching since 2008; dozens of mosques have been destroyed by mobs with police standing by. The Ahmadiyya mosque in Haifa, Israel has operated legally since 1928.
key_quote: I cannot say Assalamu Alaikum in my own country. This greeting — the greeting of peace — is illegal for me to use. Because of who I am.
israel_connection: Ahmadiyya national headquarters and mosque in Kababir neighborhood, Haifa — operating legally since 1928; community can call their worship site a mosque freely; stark contrast with Pakistan where this is a criminal act

name: Alevi Muslims
subtitle: 15–20 million people — the largest religious minority in any Muslim country, invisible to their own state
native_language: Turkish, Kurdish (Zazaki, Kurmanji) — Alevis are multiethnic
native_script: Latin (Turkey, post-1928); Cyrillic in some diaspora contexts; no distinct Alevi script
current_script: Turkish Latin script; no restriction on script but Alevi religious texts (nefes poetry) suppressed
arabization_status: N/A — Turkey is not Arab; Alevis face Sunnification/Turkification not Arabization; however Ottoman-era suppression of Alevi practices was systematic
language_vitality: Zazaki (Kurdish dialect spoken by many Alevis): endangered. Turkish: healthy. Alevi Dede oral poetry tradition: at risk.

key_destruction_events.event: Battle of Chaldiran — Ottoman Sultan Selim I massacres estimated 40,000 Alevis, calling them heretics
Dersim massacre — Turkish army kills 13,000–70,000 Alevi Kurds; thousands more deported; PM Erdogan called it 'massacre' in 2011 apology
Maraş massacre — Sunni mobs kill 100+ Alevis in three days of coordinated violence
Sivas massacre — arsonists burn Madimak Hotel during Alevi cultural festival; 35 intellectuals and artists killed; perpetrators received amnesty
Madimak Hotel in Sivas — site of the 1993 massacre — reopened as hotel; Alevi community protests desecration of massacre site

human_scale_fact: Turkey's Directorate of Religious Affairs (Diyanet) employs 80,000 Sunni imams, funds thousands of mosques, and is paid for by all Turkish taxpayers — including 15–20 million Alevis. The Diyanet does not recognize Alevi religious practice. Alevi children in Turkish state schools are required to take Sunni Islamic religious education classes — the European Court of Human Rights has ruled this violates religious freedom multiple times; Turkey has not complied. Alevi women have always prayed alongside men, unveiled. Their faith predates the Ottoman Empire's arrival in Anatolia.
key_quote: We are told we are Muslim. But our Islam has no mosque, no veil, no separation of men and women. We light candles, we play the saz, we weep for Karbala. And for this, they have always come to kill us.
israel_connection: Some Alevi diaspora in Germany have expressed solidarity with Israel; complex political alignment given Turkish government hostility to Israel under AKP

resources.label: Cumhuriyet — independent Turkish journalism on Alevis

name: Ismaili Muslims
subtitle: founded Al-Azhar. Now considered heretics by its faculty.
native_language: Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Tajik, various local languages

arabization_status: N/A — Ismailis span Arab and non-Arab contexts; face Sunnification not Arabization
language_vitality: N/A as distinct Ismaili language; Burushaski (Pakistan, spoken by some Ismailis): endangered

Gilgit massacre, Pakistan — Sunni extremists with reported Pakistani military complicity kill hundreds of Ismailis
Taliban ban Ismaili cultural and religious practices in Afghanistan; Ismaili communities in Badakhshan face forced displacement

human_scale_fact: Al-Azhar University in Cairo — the most prestigious and authoritative institution in Sunni Islam, whose fatwas are followed by millions — was founded in 970 CE by the Fatimid Ismaili Caliphate. Its founders would be considered heretics by its current faculty. The Aga Khan Development Network — the Ismaili community's global humanitarian arm — operates in 30+ countries and invests approximately $800 million annually in health, education, and poverty reduction, primarily in Muslim-majority countries.
key_quote: We are told our Imam is heresy. That our women who go to school are shameless. We have heard this for 1,200 years. We are still here.
israel_connection: No direct community; Aga Khan Development Network operates in some contexts adjacent to Israeli humanitarian initiatives

subtitle: the dominant form of popular Islam for 1,000 years — now being demolished
note_on_numbers: Sufism is a practice within Islam, not a discrete population; shrine pilgrimage involves hundreds of millions; distinct Sufi orders: millions of initiated members
native_language: Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Turkish — Sufism crosses language communities
native_script: Arabic, Persian scripts; Sufi poetry in Ottoman Turkish (now Latin script); Hausa (West Africa)
current_script: No distinct script; Sufi poetry traditions maintained in host language scripts
arabization_status: Wahhabi-funded Arabization of Islamic practice is destroying Sufi shrine culture — replacing local syncretic saint veneration with Gulf-exported puritanism
language_vitality: Sufi musical traditions (qawwali, sama, hadra) endangered by religious prohibition; Sufi poetry in endangered languages at risk

key_destruction_events.event: Saudi Arabia begins massive global export of Wahhabi Islam after Grand Mosque seizure — Sufi practices labelled bid'ah (heretical innovation)
Taliban destroy Sufi shrines across Afghanistan as 'idol worship'
Data Darbar shrine bombing, Lahore — 42 killed at shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh, 11th-century Sufi saint
Ansar Dine systematically demolishes 16 UNESCO World Heritage Sufi shrines in Timbuktu, Mali — International Criminal Court later prosecutes as war crime
Sehwan Sharif shrine bombing — 88 killed at shrine of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar (13th century); largest single Sufi massacre in Pakistan

human_scale_fact: Saudi Arabia demolished over 400 historical Islamic sites in Mecca and Medina between 1985 and 2015 — including buildings from the time of the Prophet — to build hotels, ostensibly to prevent 'idol worship' at historic sites. The Ottoman-era houses where the Prophet was born and where his companions lived are now luxury hotels and parking lots. The ICC prosecution of Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi for destroying Timbuktu's shrines was the first time the destruction of cultural heritage was prosecuted as a war crime in its own right.
key_quote: They say our music is haram. Our dancing is haram. Our love for the saints is shirk. They came and they bombed us while we were praying. While we were singing to God.
key_quote_attribution: Survivor, Sehwan Sharif shrine bombing, Pakistan, 2017
israel_connection: No direct connection; some Sufi orders historically present in Ottoman Palestine; limited contemporary relationship

name: Sexual & gender minorities
subtitle: the one minority that cuts across every other group on this list
note_on_numbers: No reliable population data — criminalization prevents self-identification; estimated 5–10% of any population applies regionally
native_language: N/A — cross-cutting identity
native_script: N/A
current_script: N/A
arabization_status: N/A — but notable: classical Arabic literature (Abbasid era), Persian poetry (Hafez, Rumi), and Ottoman court culture all contain extensive homoerotic literary traditions; the criminalization of same-sex relations is largely a 19th-century British colonial legal legacy (Section 377) and 20th-century Islamist movement, not ancient tradition
language_vitality: N/A

key_destruction_events.event: Ottoman Tanzimat reforms decriminalize same-sex relations — homosexuality was legal in the Ottoman Empire; Jordan and Turkey retain this

British India's Section 377 criminalizes 'carnal knowledge against the order of nature' — exported across British colonial possessions; Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, India (repealed 2018) all inherit this law
Iranian Islamic Revolution — homosexuality becomes capital offense; Iran executes estimated 4,000–6,000 gay men since 1979
Queen Boat raid, Cairo — Egyptian police arrest 52 men on a Nile party boat; tortured and prosecuted under debauchery laws; international outcry
Iraq criminalizes same-sex relations with up to 15 years imprisonment — reversing decades of relative tolerance

human_scale_fact: Iran executes gay men by hanging — estimated 4,000–6,000 since the Islamic Revolution. When challenged by Columbia University President Lee Bollinger in 2007, President Ahmadinejad said: 'In Iran, we don't have homosexuals like in your country.' Israel, by contrast, grants asylum to gay Palestinians, Egyptians, Iranians, and Syrians fleeing persecution. Tel Aviv has hosted Pride since 1993. Gay and lesbian soldiers serve openly in the IDF. The classical Persian poet Hafez wrote extensively of male love. The criminalization of homosexuality in much of the region is not ancient tradition — it is largely a product of British colonialism and 20th-century Islamist politics.
key_quote: I left Iran because they would have killed me. I came to Israel because here I can live as I am. My family thinks I am in Germany. They cannot know where I really am.
key_quote_attribution: Iranian gay asylum seeker, Tel Aviv, 2019
israel_connection: Israel is the only country in the Middle East where same-sex relations are fully legal; Tel Aviv Pride is one of the world's largest; Israel grants asylum to LGBTQ+ individuals from MENA countries; gay Palestinians, Egyptians, Iranians, Syrians documented as asylum recipients; IDF has no restrictions on LGBTQ+ service members

name: Buddhist civilization of Central Asia
subtitle: dominant from Afghanistan to Uzbekistan for 1,000 years. Nothing remains.
note_on_numbers: No indigenous Buddhist community anywhere in MENA or Central Asia; small expat communities (Sri Lankan, Thai workers) in Gulf states are not indigenous; this entry documents a civilization, not a living community
native_language: Gandhari Prakrit (primary Buddhist liturgical language of the region), Sanskrit, Sogdian, Bactrian, Tocharian
native_script: Kharosthi (indigenous to Gandhara — invented in the region, now extinct); Brahmi; Sogdian; Bactrian Greek
current_script: All extinct — Arabic script replaced every other writing system in the region
arabization_status: Total and complete — every place name, institutional name, cultural marker, and script was replaced; the word 'Balkh' replaced the Buddhist city of 'Bactra'; 'Bamiyan' retains its pre-Islamic name but its meaning is lost; Kharosthi script extinct
language_vitality: Gandhari Prakrit: extinct. Sogdian: extinct. Bactrian: extinct. Kharosthi script: extinct. All languages of Buddhist Central Asia have been entirely replaced.

key_destruction_events.event: Arab conquest of Persia begins — Buddhist monasteries in Khorasan burned; monks killed or flee east to India and Tibet
Umayyad campaigns in Bactria (Afghanistan) and Sogdia (Uzbekistan) — Buddhist universities destroyed; 'Nava Vihara' monastery in Balkh (largest in Central Asia) looted and burned
Mahmud of Ghazni's first campaign into Buddhist/Hindu Gandhara — 17 campaigns total; explicitly framed as jihad against idol worshippers; Somnath temple destroyed
Mongol destruction of Balkh — Genghis Khan levels 'the mother of cities'; what Arab conquest left standing is finished
Timur's campaigns complete the destruction of Buddhist-rooted urban civilization in Central Asia

Taliban destroy the Bamiyan Buddhas — two colossal statues carved in 544 CE and 507 CE; 55m and 38m tall; spent 25 days blowing them apart with dynamite, artillery, and anti-aircraft guns despite global outcry
Mes Aynak monastery complex — 2,600-year-old Buddhist city in Afghanistan — under threat from Chinese copper mining operation approved by Afghan government

human_scale_fact: The larger Bamiyan Buddha (Salsal, 55 meters) was carved in 554 CE — a thousand years before the Eiffel Tower was built. The Taliban spent 25 days in March 2001 destroying it using dynamite, anti-aircraft guns, and artillery, despite appeals from UNESCO, the UN Secretary-General, and Muslim countries including Egypt and Iran. The Gandharan Buddhist art style — created in modern Pakistan and Afghanistan — fused Indian Buddhist iconography with Greek artistic technique from Alexander the Great's campaigns. It is the origin of the iconic image of the meditating Buddha that spread to China, Japan, Korea, and Southeast Asia. The Afghanistan that produced this synthesis of Greek and Indian civilization no longer exists.
key_quote: When they blew up the Buddhas, they did not destroy stone. They destroyed the proof that this place was once a meeting point of civilizations. That is what they wanted to erase.
israel_connection: Israeli archaeologists and scholars have documented Gandharan art and Central Asian Buddhist history; no direct community connection
